name: Executive order of April 9, 1872 setting apart the first Colville Reservation, east of the Columbia
nations: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation (Colville, Lake, Sanpoil, Nespelem, Okanogan, Methow)
promises: The President set apart a reservation known as the Colville reservation, east of the Columbia: from the mouth of the Spokane up the Columbia to the 49th parallel, east to the Pend d'Oreille River, up it to the Idaho line, south to the Little Spokane, and down the Spokane to the start (Royce schedule).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that before 1872 white squatters had occupied substantial areas of the petitioner tribes' lands, most of them east of the Columbia within this original reservation, and that this occupation bore on moving the reservation to the west side of the river. It held that the tribes' title to their lands outside the July 2, 1872 reservation, which includes the Colville and Lakes tracts in this area, was taken without payment of compensation as of that date.

landTaken: The executive order of July 2, 1872 revoked this order and restored the tract to the public domain (Royce schedule; Docket 181 findings). Royce notes a portion was set apart again for the Spokane by executive order of January 18, 1881.
compensation: The Commission's Colville tract (130,590 acres, east of the Columbia from just below Kettle Falls to near Hunters) and Lakes tract (east of the Columbia up to the Canadian boundary) lie in this area. Its second interlocutory order of March 5, 1959 awarded the Colville Tribe $111,000.00 and the Lake Tribe $125,000.00, less offsets; the final judgment of March 1, 1960 left the Colville Tribe a net $104,600.00 after offsets. The Lake figure is damaged in both scans; $125,000.00 is the only reading under which the five awards ($1,061,000.00) less the $61,000.00 offsets equal the $1,000,000.00 total net recovery the 1960 judgment states.

nationVoice.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation
nationVoice.summary: The Tribes' 2023 history records that the April 1872 Presidential Executive Order established the Colville Indian Reservation for the tribes and bands who were not parties to any treaty, and that on July 2, 1872 the reservation was reduced in size.

nationVoice.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation
nationVoice.summary: The Tribes' Fish and Wildlife Department says the original Colville Reservation, set up by executive order of April 9, 1872 on the Spokane side of the Columbia, was in existence for less than three months before it was exchanged for the present reservation under the order of July 2, 1872.

openQuestions: Under the 2026-11-08 rule the July 2, 1872 revocation is not by itself a breach; this record is marked broken because the Commission found the tribes' lands, including those inside this tract, taken without compensation. The same finding is used on cession-1872-07-02-methow-okanagan and cession-1871-01-01-methow-okanagan.
treaties.json links a University of Georgia statute file (533c.pdf) for this order; it did not load, and Royce lists the order as an executive order, not a statute.
Which part of this tract each tribe held aboriginally (the Colville valley lay east of the Columbia) was not mapped against the Commission's tract findings.

Audit 2026-11-08: compensation and plain.today corrected: they gave the Methow award, but the Methow tract lies west of the Okanogan River, outside this area. The Colville and Lakes tracts, which the 1959 opinion (OSU id 191) places east of the Columbia, are the Docket 181 lands in this area, so their awards (OSU id 248; 1960 judgment id 568) replace it. The breach text no longer says the squatters were there 'with the defendant's acquiescence': that word is unreadable in finding 42. Placing the tracts in area 533 is the auditor's reading of the boundaries, not a statement of the Commission; the southern part of this tract was Spokane land (later the 1881 Spokane reservation) and the Kalispel and Spokane claims were not traced.

plain.promised: In April 1872 the President set apart a Colville Reservation east of the Columbia River, up to the Canadian line.
plain.happened: White settlers already held much of it, and in July 1872 it was revoked and moved west. The Indian Claims Commission found the tribes' lands outside the new reservation were taken without payment.
plain.today: In 1959 the Indian Claims Commission awarded $111,000.00 for the Colville lands and $125,000.00 for the Lake lands in this area, less offsets.
